entries.987b21928c2f5e23e62fca30e06a0f38047aeb9a: <div sID="gen16964" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="61" osisID="Isa.61" sID="Isa.61"/> <div eID="gen16964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16965" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16966" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. We are sure to find the grace of Christ, published by himself to a lost world in the everlasting gospel, under the type and figure of Isaiah's province, which was to foretel the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. We think we find the glories of the church of Christ, its spiritual glories, described under the type and figure of the Jews' prosperity after their return out of their captivity. 1. It is promised that they decays of the church shall be repaired, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">ver. 4</reference>. 2. That those from without shall be made serviceable to the church, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.5">ver. 5</reference>. 3. That the church shall be a royal priesthood, maintained by the riches of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">ver. 6</reference>. 4. That she shall have honour and joy in lieu of all her shame and sorrow, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">ver. 7</reference>. 5. That her affairs shall prosper, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.8">ver. 8</reference>. 6. That prosperity shall enjoy these blessings, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">ver. 9</reference>. 7. That righteousness and salvation shall be the eternal matter of the church's rejoicing and thanksgiving, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10-Isa.61.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. If the Jewish church was ever thus blessed, much more shall the Christian church be so, and all that belong to it.
entries.597c02b1b0bf21f8b175767a839b6eb9629393ca: <div eID="gen16966" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16965" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Office of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The Spirit of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon me; because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> bound; <hi type="super">2</hi> To proclaim the acceptable year of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn; <hi type="super">3</hi> To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he might be glorified. <div eID="gen16967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16968" type="x-p"/> He that is the best expositor of scripture has no doubt given us the best exposition of these verses, even our Lord Jesus himself, who read this in the synagogue at Nazareth (perhaps it was the lesson for the day) and applied it entirely to himself, saying, <hi type="italic">This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.17-Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 17, 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.21">21</reference>); and the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, in the opening of this text, were admired by all that heard them. As Isaiah was authorized and directed to proclaim liberty to the Jews in Babylon, so was Christ, God's messenger, to publish a more joyful jubilee to a lost world. And here we are told, <div eID="gen16968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16969" type="x-p"/> I. How he was fitted and qualified for this work: <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">v. 1</reference>. The prophets had the Spirit of God moving them at times, both instructing them what to say and exciting them to say it. Christ had the Spirit always resting on him without measure; but to the same intent that the prophets had, as a Spirit of counsel and a Spirit of courage, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.3">ch. xi. 1-3</reference>. When he entered upon the execution of his prophetical office the Spirit, as a dove, <hi type="italic">descended upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Matt. iii. 16</reference>. This Spirit which was upon him he communicated to those whom he sent to proclaim the same glad tidings, saying to them, when he gave them their commission, <hi type="italic">Receive you the Holy Ghost,</hi> thereby ratifying it. <div eID="gen16969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16970" type="x-p"/> II. How he was appointed and ordained to it: <hi type="italic">The Spirit of God is upon me, because the Lord God has anointed me.</hi> What service God called him to he furnished him for; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he gave him his Spirit, because he had by a sacred and solemn unction set him apart to this great office, as kings and priests were of old destined to their offices by anointing. Hence the Redeemer was called the <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> because he was <hi type="italic">anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. He has sent me;</hi> our Lord Jesus did not go unsent; he had a commission from him that is the fountain of power; <hi type="italic">the Father sent him</hi> and <hi type="italic">gave him commandment.</hi> This is a great satisfaction to us, that, whatever Christ said, he had a warrant from heaven for; his doctrine was not his, but his that sent him. <div eID="gen16970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16971" type="x-p"/> III. What the work was to which he was appointed and ordained. <div eID="gen16971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16972" type="x-p"/> 1. He was to be a preacher, was to execute the office of a prophet. So well pleased was he with the good-will God showed towards men through him that he would himself be the preacher of it, that an honour might thereby be put upon the ministry of the gospel and the faith of the saints might be confirmed and encouraged. He must preach <hi type="italic">good tidings</hi> (so <hi type="italic">gospel</hi> signified) <hi type="italic">to the meek,</hi> to the penitent, and humble, and poor in spirit; to them the tidings of a Redeemer will be indeed good tidings, pure gospel, <hi type="italic">faithful sayings, and worthy of all acceptation.</hi> The poor are commonly best disposed to receive the gospel (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jam. ii. 5</reference>), and it is likely to profit us when it is received with meekness, as it ought to be; to such Christ preached good tidings when he said, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the meek.</hi> <div eID="gen16972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> 2. He was to be a healer. He was sent to <hi type="italic">bind up the broken-hearted,</hi> as pained limbs are rolled to give them ease, as broken bones and bleeding wounds are bound up, that they may knit and close again. Those whose hearts are broken for sin, who are truly humbled under the sense of guilt and dread of wrath, are furnished in the gospel of Christ with that which will make them easy and silence their fears. Those only who have experienced the pains of a penitential contrition may expect the pleasure of divine cordials and consolations. <div eID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> 3. He was to be a deliverer. He was sent as a prophet to preach, as a priest to heal, and as a king to issue out proclamations and those of two kinds:—(1.) Proclamations of peace to his friends: He shall <hi type="italic">proclaim liberty to the captives</hi> (as Cyrus did to the Jews in captivity) and the <hi type="italic">opening of the prison to those that were bound.</hi> Whereas, by the guilt of sin, we are bound over to the justice of God, are his lawful captives, sold for sin till payment be made of that great debt, Christ lets us know that he has made satisfaction to divine justice for that debt, that his satisfaction is accepted, and if we will plead that, and depend upon it, and make over ourselves and all we have to him, in a grateful sense of the kindness he has done us, we may by faith sue out our pardon and take the comfort of it; there is, and shall be, <hi type="italic">no condemnation to us.</hi> And whereas, by the dominion of sin in us, we are bound under the power of Satan, sold under sin, Christ lets us know that he has conquered Satan, has <hi type="italic">destroyed him that had the power of death and his works,</hi> and provided for us grace sufficient to enable us to shake off the yoke of sin and to loose ourselves from <hi type="italic">those bands of our neck. The Son</hi> is ready by his Spirit to <hi type="italic">make us free;</hi> and then we shall be <hi type="italic">free indeed,</hi> not only discharged from the miseries of captivity, but advanced to all the immunities and dignities of citizens. This is the gospel proclamation, and it is like the blowing of the jubilee-trumpet, which proclaimed the great year of release (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev. xxv. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.40">40</reference>), in allusion to which it is here called <hi type="italic">the acceptable year of the Lord,</hi> the time of our acceptance with God, which is the origin of our liberties; or it is called the <hi type="italic">year of the Lord</hi> because it publishes his free grace, to his own glory, and an <hi type="italic">acceptable year</hi> because it brings glad tidings to us, and what cannot but be very acceptable to those who know the capacities and necessities of their own souls. (2.) Proclamations of war against his enemies. Christ proclaims <hi type="italic">the day of vengeance of our God,</hi> the vengeance he takes, [1.] On sin and Satan, death and hell, and all the powers of darkness, that were to be destroyed in order to our deliverances; these Christ triumphed over in his cross, having spoiled and weakened them, shamed them, and <hi type="italic">made a show of them openly,</hi> therein taking vengeance on them for all the injury they had done both to God and man, <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. [2.] On those of the children of men that stand it out against those fair offers. They shall not only be left, as they deserve, in their captivity, but be dealt with as enemies; we have the gospel summed up, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>, where that part of it, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall be saved,</hi> proclaims <hi type="italic">the acceptable year of the Lord</hi> to those that will accept of it; but the other part, <hi type="italic">He that believes not shall be damned,</hi> proclaims <hi type="italic">the day of vengeance of our God,</hi> that vengeance which he will take on those that <hi type="italic">obey not the gospel of Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> 4. He was to be a comforter, and so he is as preacher, healer, and deliverer; he is sent to <hi type="italic">comfort all who mourn,</hi> and who, mourning, seek to him, and not to the world, for comfort. Christ not only provides comfort for them, and proclaims it, but he applies it to them; he does by his Spirit comfort them. There is enough in him to <hi type="italic">comfort all who mourn,</hi> whatever their sore or sorrow is; but this comfort is sure to those who <hi type="italic">mourn in Zion,</hi> who sorrow <hi type="italic">after a godly sort,</hi> according to God, for his residence is in Zion,—who <hi type="italic">mourn because of Zion's</hi> calamities and desolations, and mingle their tears by a holy sympathy with those of all God's suffering people, though they themselves are not in trouble; such tears God has <hi type="italic">a bottle</hi> for (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Ps. lvi. 8</reference>), such mourners he has comfort in store for. As <hi type="italic">blessings out of Zion</hi> are spiritual blessings, so <hi type="italic">mourners in Zion</hi> are holy mourners, such as carry their sorrows to the throne of grace (for in Zion was the mercy-seat) and pour them out as Hannah did before the Lord. To such as these Christ has appointed by his gospel, and will give by his Spirit (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">v. 3</reference>), those consolations which will not only support them under their sorrows, but turn them into songs of praise. He will give them, (1.) <hi type="italic">Beauty for ashes.</hi> Whereas they lay in ashes, as was usual in times of great mourning, they shall not only be raised out of their dust, but made to look pleasant. Note, The holy cheerfulness of Christians is their beauty and a great ornament to their profession. Here is an elegant <hi type="italic">paronomasia</hi> in the original: He will give them <hi type="italic">pheer—beauty,</hi> for <hi type="italic">epher—ashes;</hi> he will turn their sorrow into joy as quickly and as easily as you can transpose a letter; for he speaks, and it is done. (2.) <hi type="italic">The oil of joy,</hi> which <hi type="italic">make the face to shine,</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">mourning,</hi> which <hi type="italic">disfigures the countenance</hi> and makes it unlovely. this <hi type="italic">oil of joy</hi> the saints have from that <hi type="italic">oil of gladness</hi> with which Christ himself was <hi type="italic">anointed above his fellows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">Heb. i. 9</reference>. (3.) <hi type="italic">The garments of praise,</hi> such beautiful garments as were worn on thanksgiving-days, instead of the <hi type="italic">spirit of heaviness, dimness,</hi> or <hi type="italic">contraction</hi>—open joys for secret mournings. The <hi type="italic">spirit of heaviness</hi> they keep to themselves (Zion's mourners <hi type="italic">weep in secret</hi>); but the joy they are recompensed with they are clothed with as with a garment in the eye of others. Observe, Where God gives the oil of joy he gives the garment of praise. Those comforts which come from God dispose the heart to, and enlarge the heart in, thanksgivings to God. Whatever we have the joy of God must have the praise and glory of. <div eID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> 5. He was to be a planter; for the church is God's husbandry. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he will do all this for his people, will cure their wounds, release them out of bondage, and comfort them in their sorrows, <hi type="italic">that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord,</hi> that they may be such and be acknowledged to be such, that they may be ornaments to God's vineyard and may be <hi type="italic">fruitful in the fruits of righteousness,</hi> as the branches of <hi type="italic">God's planting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">ch. lx. 21</reference>. All that Christ does for us is to make us God's people, and some way serviceable to him as living trees, <hi type="italic">planted in the house of the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">flourishing in the courts of our God;</hi> and all this <hi type="italic">that he may be glorified</hi>—that we may be brought to glorify him by a sincere devotion and an exemplary conversation (for <hi type="italic">herein is our Father glorified, that we bring forth much fruit</hi>), that others also may take occasion from God's favour shining on his people, and his grace shining in them, to praise him, and that he may be for ever <hi type="italic">glorified in his saints.</hi>
entries.e8809a5b6e08eab8066c75d57b87a11144c36310: <div eID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Office of the Messiah; The Prosperity of the Church. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations. <hi type="super">5</hi> And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> your ploughmen and your vinedressers. <hi type="super">6</hi> But ye shall be named the Priests of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall call you the Ministers of our God: ye shall eat the riches of the Gentiles, and in their glory shall ye boast yourselves. <hi type="super">7</hi> For your shame <hi type="italic">ye shall have</hi> double; and <hi type="italic">for</hi> confusion they shall rejoice in their portion: therefore in their land they shall possess the double: everlasting joy shall be unto them. <hi type="super">8</hi> For I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them. <hi type="super">9</hi> And their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they <hi type="italic">are</hi> the seed <hi type="italic">which</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath blessed. <div eID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> Promises are here made to the Jews now returned out of captivity, and settled again in their own land, which are to be extended to the gospel church, and all believers, who through grace are delivered out of spiritual thraldom; for they are capable of being spiritually applied. <div eID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> I. It is promised that their houses shall be rebuilt (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">v. 4</reference>), that their cities shall be raised out of the ruins in which they had long lain, and be fitted up for their use again: <hi type="italic">They shall build the old wastes;</hi> the <hi type="italic">old wastes</hi> shall be built, the <hi type="italic">waste cities shall be repaired,</hi> the <hi type="italic">former desolations,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the desolations of many generations,</hi> which it was feared would never be repaired, shall be <hi type="italic">raised up.</hi> The setting up of Christianity in the world repaired the decays of natural religion and raised up those desolations both of piety and honesty which had been for many generations the reproach of mankind. An unsanctified soul is like a city that is broken down and has no walls, like a house in ruins; but by the power of Christ's gospel and grace it is repaired, it is put in order again, and fitted to be a habitation of God through the Spirit. And <hi type="italic">they</hi> shall do this, those that are released out of captivity; for we are brought out of the house of bondage that we may serve God, both in building up ourselves to his glory and in helping to build up his church on earth. <div eID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16980" type="x-p"/> II. Those that were so lately servants themselves, working for their oppressors and lying at their mercy, shall now have servants to do their work for them and be at their command, not of their brethren (they are all the Lord's freemen), but of <hi type="italic">the strangers, and the sons of the alien,</hi> who shall <hi type="italic">keep their sheep, till their ground,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dress their gardens,</hi> the ancient employments of Abel, Cain, and Adam: <hi type="italic">Strangers shall feed your flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.5">v. 5</reference>. When, by the grace of God, we attain to a holy indifference as to all the affairs of this world, <hi type="italic">buying as though we possessed not</hi>—when, though our hands are employed about them, our hearts are not entangled with them, but reserved entire for God and his service—then <hi type="italic">the sons of the alien are our ploughmen and vine-dressers.</hi> <div eID="gen16980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16981" type="x-p"/> III. They shall not only be released out of their captivity, but highly preferred and honourably employed (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">v. 6</reference>): "While the strangers are <hi type="italic">keeping your flocks,</hi> you shall be keeping <hi type="italic">the charge of the sanctuary;</hi> instead of being slaves to your task-masters, <hi type="italic">you shall be named the priests of the Lord,</hi> a high and holy calling." Priests were princes' peers, and in Hebrew were called by the same name. You <hi type="italic">shall be the ministers of our God,</hi> as the Levites were. Note, Those whom God sets at liberty he sets to work; he <hi type="italic">delivers them out of the hands of their enemies</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">serve him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>. But his service is perfect freedom, nay, it is the greatest honour. When God brought Israel out of Egypt he took them to be to him a <hi type="italic">kingdom of priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exod. xix. 6</reference>. And the gospel church is a <hi type="italic">royal priesthood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. ii. 9</reference>. All believers are made to our God kings and priests; and they ought to conduct themselves as such in their devotions and in their whole conversation, with <hi type="italic">holiness to the Lord</hi> written upon their foreheads, that men may <hi type="italic">call them the priests of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen16981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16982" type="x-p"/> IV. The wealth and honour of the Gentile converts shall redound to the benefit and credit of the church, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Gentiles</hi> shall be brought into the church. Those that were strangers shall become <hi type="italic">fellow-citizens with the saints;</hi> and with themselves they shall bring all they have, to be devoted to the glory of God and used in his service; and the priests, the Lord's ministers, shall have the advantage of it. It will be a great strengthening and quickening, as well as a comfort and encouragement, to all good Christians, to see the Gentiles serving the interests of God's kingdom. 1. They shall <hi type="italic">eat the riches of the Gentiles,</hi> not which they have themselves seized by violence, but which are fairly and honourably presented to them, as <hi type="italic">gifts brought to the altar,</hi> which the priests and their families lived comfortably upon. It is not said, "You shall <hi type="italic">hoard the riches of the Gentiles,</hi> and treasure them," but, "You shall <hi type="italic">eat them;</hi>" for there is nothing better in riches than to use them and to do good with them. 2. They shall <hi type="italic">boast themselves in their glory.</hi> Whatever was the honour of the Gentiles converts before their conversion—their nobility, estates, learning, virtue, or places of trust and power—it shall all turn to the reputation of the church to which they have joined themselves; and whatever is their glory after their conversion—their holy zeal and strictness of conversation, their usefulness, their patient suffering, and all the displays of that blessed change which divine grace has made in them—shall be very much for the glory of God and therefore all good men shall glory in it. <div eID="gen16982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16983" type="x-p"/> V. They shall have abundance of comfort and satisfaction in their own bosoms, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">v. 7</reference>. The Jews no doubt were thus privileged after their return; they were in a new world, and now knew how to value their liberty and property, the pleasures of which were continually fresh and blooming. Much more do all those rejoice whom Christ has brought into the glorious liberty of God's children, especially when the privileges of their adoption shall be completed in the resurrection of the body. 1. <hi type="italic">They shall rejoice in their portion;</hi> they shall not only have their own again, but (which is a further gift of God) they shall have the comfort of it, and a heart to rejoice in it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Eccl. iii. 13</reference>. Though the houses of the returned Jews, as well as their temple, be much inferior to what they were before the captivity, yet they shall be well pleased with them and thankful for them. It is a portion <hi type="italic">in their land,</hi> their own land, the holy land, Immanuel's land, and therefore they shall rejoice in it, having so lately known what it was to be <hi type="italic">strangers in a strange land.</hi> Those that have God and heaven for their portion have reason to say that they have a worthy portion and to rejoice in it. 2. <hi type="italic">Everlasting joy shall be unto them,</hi> that is, a joyful state of their people, which shall last long, much longer than the captivity had lasted. Yet that joy of the Jewish nation was so much allayed, so often interrupted, and so soon brought to an end, that we must look for the accomplishment of this promise in the spiritual joy which believers have in God and the eternal joy they hope for in heaven. 3. This shall be a double recompence to them, and more than double, for all the reproach and vexation they have lain under in the land of their captivity: "<hi type="italic">For your shame you shall have double</hi> honour, and <hi type="italic">in your land</hi> you <hi type="italic">shall possess double</hi> wealth, to what you lost; the blessing of God upon it, and the comfort you shall have in it, shall make an abundant reparation for all the damages you have received. You shall be owned not only as <hi type="italic">God's sons,</hi> but as his <hi type="italic">first-born</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Exod. iv. 22</reference>), and therefore entitled to a double portion." As the miseries of their captivity were so great that in them they are said to have received <hi type="italic">double for all their sins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">ch. xl. 2</reference>), so the joys of their return shall be so great that in them they shall receive <hi type="italic">double for all their shame.</hi> The former is applicable to the fulness of Christ's satisfaction, in which God received <hi type="italic">double for all our sins;</hi> the latter to the fulness of heaven's joys, in which we shall receive more than <hi type="italic">double for all our services</hi> and sufferings. Job's case illustrates this: when God <hi type="italic">turned again his captivity,</hi> he gave him <hi type="italic">twice as much as he had before.</hi> <div eID="gen16983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16984" type="x-p"/> VI. God will be their faithful guide and a God in covenant with them (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will direct their work in truth.</hi> God by his providence will order their affairs for the best, according to the word of his truth. He will guide them in the ways of true prosperity, by the rules of true policy. He will by his grace direct the works of good people in the right way, the true way that leads to happiness; he will direct them to be done in sincerity and then they are pleasing to him. God <hi type="italic">desires truth in the inward parts;</hi> and, if we do our works in truth, he will <hi type="italic">make an everlasting covenant with us;</hi> for to those that <hi type="italic">walk before him</hi> and <hi type="italic">are upright</hi> he will certainly be a <hi type="italic">God all-sufficient.</hi> Now, as a reason both of this and of the foregoing promise, that God will recompense to them <hi type="italic">double for their shame,</hi> those words come in, in the former part of the verse, <hi type="italic">I the Lord love judgment.</hi> He loves that judgment should be done among men, both between magistrates and subjects and between neighbour and neighbour, and therefore he hates all injustice; and, when wrongs are done to his people by their oppressors and persecutors, he is displeased with them, not only because they are done to his people, but because they are wrongs, and against the eternal rules of equity. If men do not do justice, he loves to do judgment himself in giving redress to those that suffer wrong and punishing those that do wrong. God pleads his people's injured cause, not only because he is jealous for them, but because he is jealous for justice. To illustrate this, it is added that he <hi type="italic">hates robbery for burnt-offering.</hi> He hates injustice even in his own people, who honour him with what they have in their burnt-offerings, much more does he hate it when it is against his own people; if he hates robbery when it is for burnt-offerings to himself, much more when it is for burnt-offerings to idols, and when not only his people are robbed of their estates, but he is robbed of his offerings. It is a truth much to the honour of God that ritual services will never atone for the violation of moral precepts, nor will it justify any man's robbery to say, "It was for burnt-offerings," or <hi type="italic">Corban—It is a gift.</hi> Behold, <hi type="italic">to obey is better than sacrifice,</hi> to <hi type="italic">do justly and love mercy</hi> better than <hi type="italic">thousands of rams;</hi> nay, that robbery is most of all hateful to God which is covered with this pretence, for it makes the righteous God to be the patron of unrighteousness. Some make this a reason of the rejection of the Jews upon the bringing in of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">v. 6</reference>), because they were so corrupt in their morals, and, while they tithed mint and cummin, made nothing of <hi type="italic">judgment and mercy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Matt. xxiii. 23</reference>), whereas <hi type="italic">God loves judgment</hi> and insists upon that, and he hates both <hi type="italic">robbery for burnt offerings</hi> and <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings for robbery</hi> too, as that of the Pharisees, who made long prayers that they might the more plausibly devour widows' houses. Others read these words thus: <hi type="italic">I hate rapine by iniquity,</hi> that is, the spoil which the enemies of God's people had unjustly made of them; God hated this, and therefore would reckon with them for it. <div eID="gen16984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16985" type="x-p"/> VII. God will entail a blessing upon their posterity after them (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their seed</hi> (the children of those persons themselves that are now the blessed of the Lord, or their successors in profession, the church's seed) shall be <hi type="italic">accounted to the Lord for a generation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.30">Ps. xxii. 30</reference>. 1. They shall signalize themselves and make their neighbours to take notice of them: <hi type="italic">They shall be known among the Gentiles,</hi> shall distinguish themselves by the gravity, seriousness, humility, and cheerfulness of their conversation, especially by that brotherly love by which all men shall know them to be Christ's disciples. And, they thus distinguishing themselves, God shall dignify them, by making them the blessings of their age and instruments of his glory, and by giving them remarkable tokens of his favour, which shall make them eminent and gain them respect from all about them. Let the children of godly parents love in such a manner that they may be known to be such, that all who observe them may see in them the fruits of a good education, and an answer to the prayers that were put up for them; and then they may expect that God will make them known, by the fulfilling of that promise to them, that <hi type="italic">the generation of the upright shall be blessed.</hi> 2. God shall have the glory of this, for every one shall attribute it to the blessing of God; all that see them shall see so much of the grace of God in them, and his favour towards them, that they shall <hi type="italic">acknowledge them to be the seed which the Lord has blessed</hi> and doth bless, for it includes both. See what it is to be blessed of God. Whatever good appears in any it must be taken notice of as the fruit of God's blessing and he must be glorified in it.
entries.eff443056fca2fd19559ce00f9602c2d209a62b7: <div eID="gen16985" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prosperity of the Church. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16986" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> I will greatly rejoice in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh <hi type="italic">himself</hi> with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth <hi type="italic">herself</hi> with her jewels. <hi type="super">11</hi> For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth; so the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations. <div eID="gen16986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16987" type="x-p"/> Some make this the song of joy and praise to be sung by the prophet in the name of Jerusalem, congratulating her on the happy change of her circumstances in the accomplishment of the foregoing promises; others make it to be spoken by Christ in the name of the New-Testament church triumphing in gospel grace. We may take in both, the former as a type of the latter. We are here taught to rejoice with holy joy, to God's honour, 1. In the beginning of this good work, the clothing of the church <hi type="italic">with righteousness and salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">v. 10</reference>. Upon this account <hi type="italic">I will greatly rejoice in the Lord.</hi> Those that rejoice in God have cause to rejoice greatly, and we need not fear running into an extreme in the greatness of our joy when we make God the gladness of our joy. The first gospel song begins like this, <hi type="italic">My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.46-Luke.1.47">Luke i. 46, 47</reference>. There is just matter for this joy, and all the reason in the world why it should terminate in God; for salvation and righteousness are wrought out and brought in, and the church is clothed with them. The salvation God wrought for the Jews, and that righteousness of his in which he appeared for them, and that reformation which appeared among them, made them look as glorious in the eyes of all wise men as if they had been clothed in robes of state or nuptial garments. Christ has clothed his church with an eternal salvation (and that is truly great) by clothing it with the righteousness both of justification and sanctification. The <hi type="italic">clean linen is the righteousness of saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>. Observe how these two are put together; those, and those only, shall be clothed with the garments of salvation hereafter that are covered with the robe of righteousness now: and those garments are rich and splendid clothing, like the priestly garments (for so the word signifies) with which the <hi type="italic">bridegroom decks himself.</hi> The brightness of the sun itself is compared to them. <reference osisRef="Ps.19.5">Ps. xix. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">He is as a bridegroom</hi> coming out of his chamber, completely dressed. Such is the beauty of God's grace in those that are clothed with the robe of righteousness, that by the righteousness of Christ are recommended to God's favour and by the sanctification of the Spirit have God's image renewed upon them; they are decked as a bride to be espoused to God, and taken into covenant with him; they are decked as a priest to be employed for God, and taken into communion with him. 2. In the progress and continuance of this good work, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">v. 11</reference>. It is not like a day of triumph, which is glorious for the present, but is soon over. No; the righteousness and salvation with which the church is clothed are durable clothing; so they are said to be, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">ch. xxiii. 18</reference>. The church, when she is pleasing herself with the righteousness and salvation that Jesus Christ has clothed her with, rejoices to think that these inestimable blessings shall both spring for future ages and spread to distant regions. (1.) They shall spring forth for ages to come, as the fruits of the earth which are produced very year, from generation to generation. <hi type="italic">As the earth,</hi> even that which lies common, <hi type="italic">brings forth her bud,</hi> the tender grass at the return of the year, and as <hi type="italic">the garden</hi> enclosed <hi type="italic">causes the things that are sown in it to spring forth</hi> in their season, so duly, so constantly, so powerfully, and with such advantage to mankind <hi type="italic">will the Lord God cause righteousness and praise to spring forth,</hi> by virtue of the covenant of grace, as, in the former case, by virtue of the covenant of providence. See what the promised blessings are—<hi type="italic">righteousness and praise</hi> (for those that are clothed with righteousness <hi type="italic">show forth the praises</hi> of him that clothed them); these shall spring forth under the influence of the dew of divine grace. Though it may sometimes be winter with the church, when those blessings seem to wither and do not appear, yet the root of them is fixed, a spring-time will come, when through the reviving beams of the approaching Sun of righteousness they shall flourish again. (2.) They shall spread far, and <hi type="italic">spring forth before all the nations;</hi> the great salvation shall be published and proclaimed to all the world and the ends of the earth shall see it.  <chapter eID="Isa.61"/> <div eID="gen16987" type="x-p"/>

entries.87638a4417e9150a0fffa5c16deb1e07509e0fe1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9470"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 61</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.11">Is 61:1-11</reference>. Messiah's Offices: Restoration of Israel.</title> <div sID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> Messiah announces His twofold commission to bring gospel mercy at His first coming, and judgments on unbelievers and comfort to Zion at His second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.9">Is 61:1-9</reference>); the language can be applied to Isaiah, comforting by his prophecies the exiles in Babylon, only in a subordinate sense.<div eID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9470"/><hi type="bold">1. is upon me; because ... hath anointed me--</hi>quoted by Jesus as His credentials in preaching (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.18-Luke.4.21">Lu 4:18-21</reference>). The Spirit is upon Me in preaching, because Jehovah hath anointed Me from the womb (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Lu 1:35</reference>), and at baptism, with the Spirit "without measure," and permanently "abiding" on Me (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Is 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.32">Joh 1:32</reference>; 3:34; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; with which compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Ki 1:39</reference>, 40; 19:16; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.7">Ex 29:7</reference>). "Anointed" as Messiah, Prophet, Priest, and King.<div eID="gen16483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good tidings--</hi>as the word "gospel" means.<div eID="gen16484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the meek--</hi>rather, "the poor," as <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Lu 4:18</reference> has it; that is, those afflicted with calamity, poor in circumstances and in spirit (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Mt 11:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">proclaim liberty--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.8.31-John.8.36">Joh 8:31-36</reference>). Language drawn from the deliverance of the Babylonian captives, to describe the deliverance from sin and death (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.15">He 2:15</reference>); also from the "liberty proclaimed" to all bond-servants in the year of jubilee (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Is 61:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10">Le 25:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.8">Jr 34:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen16486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opening of the prison--</hi>The Hebrew rather is, "the most complete opening," namely, of the eyes to them that are bound, that is, deliverance from prison, for captives are as it were blind in the darkness of prison (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Is 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">35:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">42:7</reference>) [Ewald]. So <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Lu 4:18</reference> and the Septuagint interpret it; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Lu 4:18</reference>, under inspiration, adds to this, for the fuller explanation of the single clause in the Hebrew, "to set at liberty them that are bruised"; thus expressing the double "opening" implied; namely, that of the eyes (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">Joh 9:39</reference>), and that of the prison (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.18">Ro 6:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.15">He 2:15</reference>). His miracles were acted parables. <div eID="gen16487" type="x-p"/>
entries.600b09e35ab111d96f7c12b82ce78cf5b7787fba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9471"/><div sID="gen16488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9471"/><hi type="bold">2. acceptable year--</hi>the year of jubilee on which "liberty was proclaimed to the captives" (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of vengeance--</hi>The "acceptable time of grace" is a "year"; the time of "vengeance" but "a day" (so <reference osisRef="Isa.34.8">Is 34:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.4">63:4</reference>; Mal 4:1). Jesus (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.20">Lu 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.21">21</reference>) "closed the book" before this clause; for the interval from His first to His second coming is "the acceptable year"; the day of vengeance" will not be till He comes again (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7-2Thess.1.9">2Th 1:7-9</reference>).<div eID="gen16489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our God--</hi>The saints call Him "our God"; for He cometh to "avenge" them (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.10">Re 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.2">19:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that mourn--</hi>The "all" seems to include the spiritual Israelite mourners, as well as the literal, who are in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference> called "them that mourn in Zion," and to whom <reference osisRef="Isa.57.18">Is 57:18</reference> refers. <div eID="gen16491" type="x-p"/>
entries.4735d18a3a3721f44fcaece8cac9f57813a7fe5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9472"/><div sID="gen16492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9472"/><hi type="bold">3. To appoint ... to give--</hi>The double verb, with the one and the same accusative, imparts glowing vehemence to the style.<div eID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beauty for ashes--</hi>There is a play on the sound and meaning of the Hebrew words, peer, epher, literally, "ornamental headdress" or tiara (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>), worn in times of joy, instead of a headdress of "ashes," cast on the head in mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.19">2Sa 13:19</reference>).<div eID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oil of joy--</hi>Perfumed ointment was poured on the guests at joyous feasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">45:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Am 6:6</reference>). On occasions of grief its use was laid aside (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2Sa 14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">garment of praise--</hi>bright-colored garments, indicative of thankfulness, instead of those that indicate despondency, as sackcloth (<reference osisRef="John.16.20">Joh 16:20</reference>).<div eID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trees of righteousness--</hi>Hebrew, terebinth trees; symbolical of men strong in righteousness, instead of being, as heretofore, bowed down as a reed with sin and calamity (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">30</reference>; 42:3; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.15">1Ki 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; 92:12-14; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">planting of ... Lord--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Is 60:21</reference>).<div eID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he might be glorified--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.15.8">Joh 15:8</reference>). <div eID="gen16498" type="x-p"/>

But ye--</hi>as contrasted with the "strangers." Ye shall have no need to attend to your flocks and lands: strangers will do that for you; your exclusive business will be the service of Jehovah as His "priests" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>, which remains yet to be realized; compare as to the spiritual Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Is 66:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ministers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.11">Eze 44:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat ... riches of ... Gentiles--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5-Isa.60.11">Is 60:5-11</reference>).<div eID="gen16503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their glory ... boast yourselves--</hi>rather, "in their splendor ye shall be substituted in their stead"; ye shall substitute yourselves [Maurer]. <div eID="gen16504" type="x-p"/>
entries.9abda94fcf486b2e6bc9179474a9d7c75e6d70c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9476"/><div sID="gen16505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9476"/><hi type="bold">7. double--</hi>Instead of your past share, ye shall have not merely as much, but "double" as much reward (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.12">Zec 9:12</reference>; compare the third clause in this verse).<div eID="gen16505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confusion--</hi>rather, "humiliation," or "contumely."<div eID="gen16506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice--</hi>They shall celebrate with jubilation their portion [Maurer]. Transition from the second to the third person.<div eID="gen16507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their land--</hi>marking the reference to literal Israel, not to the Church at large.<div eID="gen16508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting joy--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Is 35:10</reference>). <div eID="gen16509" type="x-p"/>

So in <reference osisRef="Job.5.6">Job 5:6</reference>. Hating, as I do, the rapine, combined with iniquity, perpetrated on My people by their enemies, I will vindicate Israel.<div eID="gen16511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">direct ... work in truth--</hi>rather, "I will give them the reward of their work" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Is 40:10</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.11">Is 62:11</reference>, Margin) in faithfulness. <div eID="gen16512" type="x-p"/>

Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>) gives thanks for God's returning favor (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.46">Lu 1:46</reference>, 47; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.18">Ha 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen16516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salvation ... righteousness--</hi>inseparably connected together. The "robe" is a loose mantle thrown over the other parts of the dress (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">Psa 132:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.4">149:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">19:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">decketh himself with ornaments--</hi>rather "maketh himself a priestly headdress," that is, a magnificent headdress, such as was worn by the high priest, namely, a miter and a plate, or crown of gold worn in front of it [Aquila, &c.]; appropriate to the "kingdom of priests," dedicated to the offering of spiritual sacrifices to God continually (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">Re 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.6">20:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jewels--</hi>rather, "ornaments" in general [Barnes]. <div eID="gen16519" type="x-p"/>
