entries.9cb8d871e1548c3310bec21f430dc25f23212aa5: <div eID="gen28906" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28907" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28908" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28908" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28907" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28909" type="x-p"/> The subject of the preceding chapter is continued in this; and to give it the greater solemnity, the Messiah is introduced describing his character and office, and confirming the large promises made before, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.9">Isa 61:1-9</reference>. In consequence of this the Jewish Church is introduced, praising God for the honor done her by her restoration to favor, and by to accession of the Gentiles, which is beautifully described by allusions to the rich pontifical dress of the high priest; a happy similitude to express the ornaments of a restored nation and of a renewed mind, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Isa 61:10</reference>. Certainty of the prophecy illustrated by a figure drawn from the vegetable kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">Isa 61:11</reference>. <div eID="gen28909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28911" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me "The Spirit of Jehovah is upon me" - The Septuagint, Vulgate, and St. Luke, (<reference osisRef="Luk.4.18">Luk 4:18</reference>), and a MS., and two old editions omit the word אדני Adonai, the Lord; which was probably added to the text through the superstition of the Jews, to prevent the pronunciation of the word יהוה Jehovah following. See Kennicott on the state of the printed Hebrew text, vol. i., p. 610. <div eID="gen28911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28912" type="x-p"/> In most of Isaiah's prophecies there is a primary and secondary sense, or a remote subject illustrated by one that is near. The deliverance of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon is constantly used to shadow forth the salvation of men by Jesus Christ. Even the prophet himself is a typical person, and is sometimes intended to represent the great Savior. It is evident from <reference osisRef="Luk.4.18">Luk 4:18</reference> that this is a prophecy of our blessed Lord and his preaching; and yet it is as evident that it primarily refers to Isaiah preaching the glad tidings of deliverance to the Jews. <div eID="gen28912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28913" type="x-p"/> The opening of the prison "Perfect liberty" - פקח קוח pekach koach. Ten MSS. of Kennicott's, several of De Rossi's, and one of my own, with the Complutensian, have פקחקוח pekachkoach in one word; and so the Septuagint and Vulgate appear to have taken it: not merely opening of prisons, but every kind of liberty - complete redemption. <div eID="gen28913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28914" type="x-p"/> The proclaiming of perfect liberty to the bound, and the year of acceptance with Jehovah. is a manifest allusion to the proclaiming of the year of jubilee by sound of trumpet. See <reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev 25:9</reference>, etc. This was a year of general release of debts and obligations, of bondmen and bondwomen, of lands and possessions which had been sold from the families and tribes to which they belonged. Our Savior, by applying this text to himself, (<reference osisRef="Luk.4.18">Luk 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.19">Luk 4:19</reference>), a text so manifestly relating to the institution above mentioned, plainly declares the typical design of that institution.
entries.ff4b99041317887c1f8341e1ed610346cd58630f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28915" type="x-p"/> To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion "To impart gladness to the mourners of Zion" - A word necessary to the sense is certainly lost in this place, of which the ancient Versions have preserved no traces. Houbigant, by conjecture, inserts the word ששון sason, gladness, taken from the line next but one below, where it stands opposed to אבל ebel, sorrow or mourning, as the word lost here was to אבלי abeley, mourners: I follow him. - L. <div eID="gen28915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28916" type="x-p"/> Beauty for ashes "A beautiful crown instead of ashes" - In times of mourning the Jews put on sackcloth, or coarse and sordid raiment, and spread dust and ashes on their heads; on the contrary, splendid clothing and ointment poured on the head were the signs of joy. "Feign thyself to be a mourner," says Joab to the woman of Tekoah, "and put on now mourning apparel, and anoint not thyself with oil," <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2Sam 14:2</reference>. These customs are at large expressed in the Book of Judith: "She pulled off the sackcloth which she had on, and put off the garments of her widowhood, and washed her body all over with water and anointed herself with precious ointment, and braided the hair of her head, and put on a tire [mitre, marg.] upon it; and put on her garments of gladness;" chap. 10:3. - L. פאר תחת אפר peer tachath ephar, glory for ashes; a paronomasia which the prophet often uses: a chaplet, crown, or other ornament of the head (for so the Vulgate renders the word here and in the both verse; in which last place the Septuagint agree in the same rendering), instead of dust and ashes, which before covered it; and the costly ointments used on occasions of festivity, instead of the ensigns of sorrow. - L. <div eID="gen28916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28917" type="x-p"/> Trees of righteousness "Trees approved" - Hebrews oaks of righteousness or truth; that is, such as by their flourishing condition should show that they were indeed "the scion of God's planting, and the work of his hands;" under which images, in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Isa 60:21</reference>, the true servants of God, in a highly improved state of the Church, were represented; that is, says Vitringa on that place, "commendable for the strength of their faith, their durability, and firmness."
entries.a072e083f1ce5080e6933629eda1e8e03efb4c45: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> "And they that spring from thee" - A word is lost here likewise. After ובנו ubanu, "they shall build," add ממך mimmecha, they that spring from thee. Four MSS. have it so, (two of them ancient), and one of mine has it in the margin, and it is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>, where the sentence is the very same, this word being here added. Kimchi makes the same remark: "the word ממך mimmecha is omitted here; but is found in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>." <div eID="gen28917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28918" type="x-p"/> The desolations of many generations - It seems that these words cannot refer to the Jews in the Balbylonish captivity, for they were not there many generations; but it may refer to their dispersions and state of ruin since the advent of our Lord; and consequently this may be a promise of the restoration of the Jewish people.
entries.3bd960712a6ec20b25802f5e9c79994ab0ffa21a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen28918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28919" type="x-p"/> Strangers shall - feed your flocks - Gentiles shall first preach to you the salvation of Christ, and feed with Divine knowledge the Jewish congregations.
entries.81e6d66a53a2f3dfe438c68ff53eb863cdfcf2bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28920" type="x-p"/> For your shame "Instead of your shame" - The translation of this verse, which is very confused, and probably corrupted in the Hebrew, is taken from the Syriac Version; except that the latter has not expressed the word משנה mishneh, double, in the first place. Five MSS. add the conjunction ו vau to שמחת simchath. The Syriac reads תרנו taronnu, and תירשו tirashu, in the second person, "ye shall rejoice, ye shall inherit. "And for להם lahem, to them, two MSS., (one of them ancient), three of De Rossi's, and the Syriac, read לכם lachem, to you, in the second person likewise. <div eID="gen28920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28921" type="x-p"/> The Version of the Septuagint is imperfect in this place; the first half of the verse is entirely omitted in all the printed copies. It is supplied by MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2 in the following manner: - Αντι της αισχυνης ὑμων της διπλης, Και αντι της εντροπης αγαλλιασεται ἡ μερις αυτων· Δια τουτο την γην αυτων εκ δευτερου- "Instead of your shame ye shall have double, <div eID="gen28921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28922" type="x-p"/> And instead of your confusion their portion shall rejoice; <div eID="gen28922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28923" type="x-p"/> Therefore, they shall possess their land a second time." <div eID="gen28923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28924" type="x-p"/> In which the two MSS. agree, except that 1. D. 2 has by mistake ἡμερας, day, for ἡ μερις, the part. And Cod. Marchal., in the margin, has pretty nearly the same supplement as from Theodotion. - L.
entries.7c7933aae317469e53bc7fdeb24979bc6812dcea: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28925" type="x-p"/> I hate robbery for burnt-offering "Who hate rapine and iniquity" - The Syriac, and Chaldee prefix the conjunction ו vau, instead of the preposition ב beth, to עולה olah, which they render iniquity or oppression; and so the Septuagint, αδικιας. The difference lies in the punctuation; בעולה beolah, in a burnt-offering בעולה beavelah, in iniquity. The letters are the same in both words. Five of De Rossi's MSS. confirm this reading.
entries.1eb3a38c8ff3ffaf06f0fcace21c0f0b8ef1101c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28926" type="x-p"/> Their seed shall be known among the Gentiles - Both Jews and Gentiles are to make but one fold under one shepherd, Christ Jesus. But still, notwithstanding this, they may retain their peculiarity and national distinction; so that though they are known to be Christians, yet they shall appear to be converted Jews. After their conversion to Christianity this will necessarily be the case for a long time. Strange nations are not so speedily amalgamated, as to lose their peculiar cast of features, and other national distinctions.
entries.17da2a904231fecaf527a00ee211f8aa00194b56: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28927" type="x-p"/> I will greatly rejoice in the Lord - These may be the words of the Jews now converted, and brought into the Church of Christ, and with the Gentiles made fellow heirs of the blessings of the new covenant. <div eID="gen28927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28928" type="x-p"/> As a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments "As the bridegroom decketh himself with a priestly crown" - An allusion to the magnificent dress of the high priest, when performing his functions; and particularly to the mitre, and crown or plate of gold on the front of it, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.6">Exo 29:6</reference>. The bonnet or mitre of the priests also was made, as Moses expresses it, "for glory and for beauty, "<reference osisRef="Exo.28.40">Exo 28:40</reference>. It is difficult to give its full force to the prophet's metaphor in another language. The version of Aquila and Symmachus comes nearest to it: ὡς νυμφιον ἱερατευομενον στεφανῳ· "as a bridegroom decked with a priestly crown." - L.
entries.70bb2dc4c37a0a021c6144508dae44e8eac9711a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28929" type="x-p"/> The Lord God "The Lord Jehovah" - "אדני Adonai, the Lord, makes the line longer than the preceding and following; and the Septuagint, Alexandrian, (and MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. II.), and Arabic, do not so render it. Hence it seems to be interpolated." - Dr. Jubb. Three MSS. have it not. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa 61:1</reference> (note). Both words אדני יהוה Adonai Jehovah, are wanting in one of my MSS.; but are supplied in the margin by a later hand.  <chapter eID="Isa.61"/> <div eID="gen28929" type="x-p"/>

entries.e085918f3de44125729e038a4b31ce4a600c976c: <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3">Isa 61:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> The words of Jehovah Himself pass over here into the words of another, whom He has appointed as the Mediator of His gracious counsel. <hi type="italic">“The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is over me, because Jehovah hath anointed me, to bring glad tidings to sufferers, hath sent me to bind up broken-hearted ones, to proclaim liberty to those led captive, and emancipation to the fettered; to proclaim a year of grace from Jehovah, and a day of vengeance from our God; to comfort all that mourn; to put upon the mourners of Zion, to give them a head-dress for ashes, oil of joy for mourning, a wrapper of renown for an expiring spirit, that they may be called terebinths of righteousness, a planting of Jehovah for glorification.”</hi> Who is the person speaking here? The Targum introduces the passage with נביּא אמר. Nearly all the modern commentators support this view. Even the closing remarks to Drechsler (iii. 381) express the opinion, that the prophet who exhibited to the church the summit of its glory in chapter 60, an evangelist of the rising from on high, an apocalyptist who sketches the painting which the New Testament apocalyptist is to carry out in detail, is here looking up to Jehovah with a grateful eye, and praising Him with joyful heart for his exalted commission. But this view, when looked at more closely, cannot possibly be sustained. It is open to the following objections: (1.) The prophet never speaks of himself as a prophet at any such length as this; on the contrary, with the exception of the closing words of <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">Isa 57:21</reference>, “saith my God,” he has always most studiously let his own person fall back into the shade. (2.) Wherever any other than Jehovah is represented as speaking, and as referring to his own calling, or his experience in connection with that calling, as in Isa 49:1., Isa 50:4., it is the very same “servant of Jehovah” of whom and to whom Jehovah speaks in Isa 42:1., Isaiah 52:13-53:12, and therefore not the prophet himself, but He who had been appointed to be the Mediator of a new covenant, the light of the Gentiles, the salvation of Jehovah for the whole world, and who would reach this glorious height, to which He had been called, through self-abasement even to death. (3.) All that the person speaking here says of himself is to be found in the picture of the unequalled “Servant of Jehovah,” who is highly exalted above the prophet. He is endowed with the Spirit of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa 42:1</reference>); Jehovah has sent Him, and with Him His Spirit (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Isa 48:16</reference></hi>); He has a tongue taught of God, to help the exhausted with words (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa 50:4</reference>); He spares and rescues those who are almost despairing and destroyed, the bruised reed and expiring wick (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">Isa 42:7</reference>). “To open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison-house:” this is what He has chiefly to do for His people, both in word and deed (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">Isa 42:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.9">Isa 49:9</reference>). (4.) We can hardly expect that, after the prophet has described the Servant of Jehovah, of whom He prophesied, as coming forward to speak with such dramatic directness as in Isa 49:1., Isa 50:4. (and even <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Isa 48:16</reference></hi>), he will now proceed to put himself in the foreground, and ascribe to himself those very same official attributes which he has already set forth as characteristic features in his portrait of the predicted One. For these reasons we have no doubt that we have here the words of the Servant of Jehovah. The glory of Jerusalem is depicted in chapter 60 in the direct words of Jehovah Himself, which are well sustained throughout. And now, just as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Isa 48:16</reference></hi>, though still more elaborately, we have by their side the words of His servant, who is the mediator of this glory, and who above all others is the pioneer thereof in his evangelical predictions. Just as Jehovah says of him in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa 42:1</reference>, “I have put my Spirit upon him;” so here he says of himself, “The Spirit of Jehovah is upon me.” And when he continues to explain this still further by saying, “because” (יען from ענה, intention, purpose; here equivalent to אשׁר יען) “Jehovah hath anointed me” (<hi type="italic">mâs</hi> <hi type="italic">'ōthı̄</hi>, more emphatic than <hi type="italic">meshâchanı̄</hi>), notwithstanding the fact that <hi type="italic">mâshach</hi> is used here in the sense of prophetic and not regal anointing (1Ki 19:16), we may find in the choice of this particular word a hint at the fact, that the Servant of Jehovah and the Messiah are one and the same person. So also the account given in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.22">Luk 4:16-22</reference> viz. that when Jesus was in the synagogue at Nazareth, after reading the opening words of this address, He closed the book with these words, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears” - cannot be interpreted more simply in any other way, than on the supposition that Jesus here declares Himself to be the predicted and divinely anointed Servant of Jehovah, who brings the gospel of redemption to His people. Moreover, though it is not decisive in favour of our explanation, yet this explanation is favoured by the fact that the speaker not only appears as the herald of the new and great gifts of God, but also as the dispenser of them (“<hi type="italic">non praeco tantum, sed et dispensator</hi>,” Vitringa). <div eID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> The combination of the names of God (<hi type="italic">'Adonai</hi> <hi type="italic">Yehovâh</hi>) is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa 50:4</reference>-9. On <hi type="italic">bissēr</hi>, εὐαγγελίζειν (-εσθαι). He comes to put a bandage on the hearts’ wounds of those who are broken-hearted: ל חבשׁ (חבּשׁ) as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.3">Psa 147:3</reference>; cf., ל רפא (רפּא); ל הצדיק. דרור קרא is the phrase used in the law for the proclamation of the freedom brought by the year of jubilee, which occurred every fiftieth year after seven sabbatical periods, and was called <hi type="italic">shenath</hi> <hi type="italic">hadderōr</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.17">Eze 46:17</reference>); <hi type="italic">deror</hi> from <hi type="italic">dârar</hi>, a verbal stem, denoting the straight, swift flight of a swallow (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Psa 84:4</reference>), and free motion in general, such as that of a flash of lightning, a liberal self-diffusion, like that of a superabundant fulness. <hi type="italic">Peqach</hi>-<hi type="italic">qōăch</hi> is written like two words (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa 2:20</reference>). The Targum translates it as if <hi type="italic">peqach</hi> were an imperative: “Come to the light,” probably meaning undo the bands. But <hi type="italic">qōăch</hi> is not a Hebrew word; for the <hi type="italic">qı̄chōth</hi> of the Mishna (the loops through which the strings of a purse are drawn, for the purpose of lacing it up) cannot be adduced as a comparison. Parchon, AE, and A, take <hi type="italic">peqachqōăch</hi> as one word (of the form פּתלתּל, שׁחרחר), in the sense of throwing open, viz., the prison. But as <hi type="italic">pâqach</hi> is never used like <hi type="italic">pâthach</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Isa 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.14">Isa 51:14</reference>), to signify the opening of a room, but is always applied to the opening of the eyes (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">Isa 35:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.7">Isa 42:7</reference>, etc.), except in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.20">Isa 42:20</reference>, where it is used for the opening of the ears, we adhere to the strict usage of the language, if we understand by <hi type="italic">peqachqōăch</hi> the opening up of the eyes (as contrasted with the dense darkness of the prison); and this is how it has been taken even by the lxx, who have rendered it καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν, as if the reading had been ולעורים (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.8">Psa 146:8</reference>). Again, he is sent to promise with a loud proclamation a year of good pleasure (<hi type="italic">râtsōn</hi>: syn. <hi type="italic">yeshū‛âh</hi>) and a day of vengeance, which Jehovah has appointed; a promise which assigns the length of a year for the thorough accomplishment of the work of grace, and only the length of a day for the work of vengeance. The vengeance applies to those who hold the people of God in fetters, and oppress them; the grace to all those whom the infliction of punishment has inwardly humbled, though they have been strongly agitated by its long continuance (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>). The <hi type="italic">'ăbhēlı̄m</hi>, whom the Servant of Jehovah has to comfort, are the “mourners of Zion,” those who take to heart the fall of Zion. In <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference>, לשׂוּם ... לתת, he corrects himself, because what he brings is not merely a diadem, to which the word <hi type="italic">sūm</hi> (to set) would apply, but an abundant supply of manifold gifts, to which only a general word like <hi type="italic">nâthan</hi> (to give) is appropriate. Instead of אפר, the ashes of mourning or repentance laid upon the head, he brings פּאר, a diadem to adorn the head (a transposition even so far as the letters are concerned, and therefore the counterpart of אפר; the”oil of joy” (from <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Psa 45:8</reference>; compare also משׁחך there with אתי משׁח here) instead of mourning; “a wrapper (cloak) of renown” instead of a faint and almost extinguished spirit. The oil with which they henceforth anoint themselves is to be joy or gladness, and renown the cloak in which they wrap themselves (a genitive connection, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference>). And whence is all this? The gifts of God, though represented in outward figures, are really spiritual, and take effect within, rejuvenating and sanctifying the inward man; they are the sap and strength, the marrow and impulse of a new life. The church thereby becomes “terebinths of righteousness” (אילי: Targ., Symm., Jer., render this, strong ones, mighty ones; Syr. <hi type="italic">dechre</hi>, rams; but though both of these are possible, so far as the letters are concerned, they are unsuitable here), i.e., possessors of righteousness, produced by God and acceptable with God, having all the firmness and fulness of terebinths, with their strong trunks, their luxuriant verdure, and their perennial foliage - a planting of Jehovah, to the end that He may get glory out of it (a repetition of <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Isa 60:21</reference>).
entries.f2b561707d5a019ae7cd1a1cbad2c55dfcb223b1: <reference osisRef="Isa.61.4-Isa.61.6">Isa 61:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> Even in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference></hi> with להם וקרא a perfect was introduced in the place of the infinitives of the object, and affirmed what was to be accomplished through the mediation of the Servant of Jehovah. The second turn in the address, which follows in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.4-Isa.61.9">Isa 61:4-9</reference>, continues the use of such perfects, which afterwards pass into futures. But the whole is still governed by the commencement in Isa 61:1. The Servant of Jehovah celebrates the glorious office committed to him, and expounds the substance of the gospel given him to proclaim. It points to the restoration of the promised land, and to the elevation of Israel, after its purification in the furnace of judgment, to great honour and dignity in the midst of the world of nations. <hi type="italic">“And they will build up wastes of the olden time, raise up desolations of the forefathers, and renew desolate cities, desolations of former generations. And strangers stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners become your ploughmen and vinedressers. But ye will be called priests of Jehovah; Servants of our God, will men say to you: ye will eat the riches of the nations, and pride yourselves in their glory.”</hi> The desolations and wastes of <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi> and <hi type="italic">dōr</hi> <hi type="italic">vâdōr</hi>, i.e., of ages remote and near (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>), are not confined to what had lain in ruins during the seventy years of the captivity. The land will be so thickly populated, that the former places of abode will not suffice (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.19-Isa.49.20">Isa 49:19-20</reference>); so that places must be referred to which are lying waste beyond the present bounds of the promised land (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Isa 54:3</reference>), and which will be rebuilt, raised up, and renewed by those who return from exile, and indeed by the latest generations (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>, מםּ; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.60.14">Isa 60:14</reference>). <hi type="italic">Chōrebh</hi>, in the sense of desolation, is a word belonging to the alter period of the language (Zeph., Jer., and Ezek.). The rebuilding naturally suggests the thought of assistance on the part of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.10">Isa 60:10</reference>). But the prophet expresses the fact that they will enter into the service of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.5">Isa 61:5</reference>), in a new and different form. They “stand there” (viz., at their posts ready for service, <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>-<hi type="italic">mish - martâm</hi>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.6">2Ch 7:6</reference>), “and feed your flocks” (צאן <hi type="italic">singularetantum</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Gen.30.43">Gen 30:43</reference>), and foreigners are your ploughmen and vinedressers. Israel is now, in the midst of the heathen who have entered into the congregation of Jehovah and become the people of God (ch <reference osisRef="Isa.19.25">Isa 19:25</reference>), what the Aaronites formerly were in the midst of Israel itself. It stands upon the height of its primary destination to be a kingdom of priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>). They are called “priests of Jehovah,” and the heathen call them “servants of our God;” for even the heathen speak with believing reverence of the God, to whom Israel renders priestly service, as “our God.” This reads as if the restored Israelites were to stand in the same relation to the converted heathen as the clergy to the laity; but it is evident, from <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Isa 66:21</reference>, that the prophet has no such hierarchical separation as this in his mind. All that we can safely infer from his prophecy is, that the nationality of Israel will not be swallowed up by the entrance of the heathen into the community of the God of revelation. The people created by Jehovah, to serve as the vehicle of the promise of salvation and the instrument in preparing the way for salvation, will also render Him special service, even after that salvation has been really effected. At the same time, we cannot take the attitude, which is here assigned to the people of sacred history after it has become the teacher of the nations, viz., as the leader of its worship also, and shape it into any clear and definite form that shall be reconcilable with the New Testament spirit of liberty and the abolition of all national party-walls. The Old Testament prophet utters New Testament prophecies in an Old Testament form. Even when he continues to say, “Ye will eat the riches of the Gentiles, and pride yourselves in their glory,” i.e., be proud of the glorious things which have passed from their possession into yours, this is merely colouring intended to strike the eye, which admits of explanation on the ground that he saw the future in the mirror of the present, as a complete inversion of the relation in which the two had stood before. The figures present themselves to him in the form of contrasts. The New Testament apostle, on the other hand, says in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Rom 11:12</reference> that the conversion of all Israel to Christ will be “the riches of the Gentiles.” But if even then the Gentile church should act according to the words of the same apostle in <reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Rom 15:27</reference>, and show her gratitude to the people whose spiritual debtor she is, by ministering to them in carnal things, all that the prophet has promised here will be amply fulfilled. We cannot adopt the explanation proposed by Hitzig, Stier, etc., “and changing with them, ye enter into their glory” (<hi type="italic">hithyammēr</hi> from <hi type="italic">yâmar</hi> = <hi type="italic">mūr</hi>, <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.: <hi type="italic">hēmı̄r</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer 2:11</reference>; lit., to exchange with one another, to enter into one another’s places); for <hi type="italic">yâmar</hi> = <hi type="italic">‛âmar</hi> (cf., <hi type="italic">yâchad</hi> = <hi type="italic">'âchad</hi>; <hi type="italic">yâsham</hi> = <hi type="italic">'âsham</hi>; <hi type="italic">yâlaph</hi> = <hi type="italic">'âlaph</hi>), to press upwards, to rise up (related to <hi type="italic">tâmar</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9">Isa 17:9</reference>; <hi type="italic">sâmar</hi>, Symm. ὀρθοτριχεῖν, possibly also <hi type="italic">‛âmar</hi> with the <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> <hi type="italic">hith‛ammēr</hi>, lxx καταδυναστεύειν), yields a much simpler and more appropriate meaning. From this verb we have <hi type="italic">hith'ammēr</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>, “to lift one’s self up (proudly),” and here <hi type="italic">hithyammēr</hi>; and it is in this way that the word has been explained by Jerome (<hi type="italic">superbietis</hi>), and possibly by the lxx (θαυμασθήσεσθε, in the sense of <hi type="italic">spectabiles eritis</hi>), by the Targum, and the Syriac, as well as by most of the ancient and modern expositors.
entries.c31783b3e0ee867b92e17e68cf5a02f5927f4b2b: <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7-Isa.61.9">Isa 61:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> The shame of banishment will then be changed into an excess of joy, and honourable distinction. <hi type="italic">“Instead of shame ye will have double, and </hi>(<hi type="italic">instead</hi>)<hi type="italic">of insult they rejoice at their portion: thus in their land they will possess double; everlasting joy will they have. For I Jehovah love right, hate robbery in wickedness; and give them their reward in faithfulness, and conclude an everlasting covenant with them. And their family will be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of the nations: all who see them will recognise them, for they are a family that Jehovah hath blessed.”</hi> The enigmatical first half of <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference> is explained in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Isa 61:2</reference>, where <hi type="italic">mishneh</hi> is shown to consist of double possession in the land of their inheritance, which has not only been restored to them, but extended far beyond the borders of their former possession; and <hi type="italic">yârōnnū</hi> <hi type="italic">chelqâm</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.65.14">Isa 65:14</reference>) denotes excessive rejoicing in the ground and soil belonging to them (according to the appointment of Jehovah): <hi type="italic">chelqâm</hi> as in Mic 2:4; and <hi type="italic">mishneh</hi> as equivalent not to כבוד משׁנה, but to ירשּׁה משׁנה. Taking this to be the relation between <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference></hi>, the meaning of <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> is not, “therefore, because they have hitherto suffered shame and reproach;” but what is promised in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference></hi> is unfolded according to its practical results, the effects consequent upon its fulfilment being placed in the foreground; so that there is less to astonish us in the elliptically brief form of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference></hi> which needed explanation. The transition from the form of address to that of declaration is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6">Isa 31:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa 52:14</reference>-15. וּכלמּה is a concise expression for כלמה ותחת, just as וּתהלּתי in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.9">Isa 48:9</reference> is for תהלתי וּלמען. <hi type="italic">Chelqâm</hi> is either the accusative of the object, according to the construction of רנּן, which occurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>; or what I prefer, looking at חמה in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>, and וּזבחיך in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.23">Isa 43:23</reference>, an adverbial accusative = בחלקם. The lxx, Jerome, and Saad. render the clause, in opposition to the accents, “instead of your double shame and reproach;” but in that case the principal words of the clause would read הלקכם תּרנּוּ. The explanation adopted by the Targum, Saad., and Jerome, “shame on the part of those who rejoice in their portion,” is absolutely impossible. The great majority of the modern commentators adopt essentially the same explanation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference></hi> as we have done, and even A. E. Kimchi does the same. Hahn’s modification, “instead of your shame is the double their portion, and (instead) of the insult this, that they will rejoice,” forces a meaning upon the syntax which is absolutely impossible. The reason for the gracious recompense for the wrong endured is given in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.8">Isa 61:8</reference>, “Jehovah loves the right,” which the enemies of Israel have so shamefully abused. “He hates בּעולה גזל, i.e., not rapinam in holocausto (as Jerome, Talmud <hi type="italic">b. Succa</hi> 30 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, Luther, and others render it; Eng. ver. “robbery for burnt-offering”) - for what object would there be in mentioning sacrifices here, seeing that only heathen sacrifices could be intended, and there would be something worse than <hi type="italic">gâzēl</hi> to condemn in them? - but <hi type="italic">robbery</hi>, or, strictly speaking, “something robbed in or with knavery” (lxx, Targ., Syr., Saad.), which calls to mind at once the cruel robbery or spoiling that Israel had sustained from the Chaldeans, its <hi type="italic">bōzezı̄m</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.24">Isa 42:24</reference>) - a robbery which passed all bounds. עולה is softened from עולה (from עול, עול), like עלתה in <reference osisRef="Job.5.16">Job 5:16</reference>, and עולת in <reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Psa 58:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.64.7">Psa 64:7</reference>; though it is doubtful whether the punctuation assumes the latter, as the Targum does, and not rather the meaning <hi type="italic">holocaustum</hi> supported by the <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi>. For the very reason, therefore, that Israel had been so grievously ill-treated by the instruments of punishment employed by Jehovah, He would give those who had been ill-treated their due reward, after He had made the evil, which He had not approved, subservient to His own salutary purposes. פּעלּה is the reward of work in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Lev 19:13</reference>, of hardship in <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.20">Eze 29:20</reference>; here it is the reward of suffering. This reward He would give בּאמת, exactly as He had promised, without the slightest deduction. The posterity of those who have been ill-treated and insulted will be honourably known (נודע as in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.23">Pro 31:23</reference>) in the world of nations, and men will need only to catch sight of them to recognise them (by prominent marks of blessing), for they are a family blessed of God. כּי, not <hi type="italic">quod</hi> (because), although it might have this meaning, but nam (for), as in <reference osisRef="Gen.27.23">Gen 27:23</reference>, since <hi type="italic">hikkı̄r</hi> includes the meaning <hi type="italic">agnoscere</hi> (to recognise).
entries.cf9c6fb28287a2546c9ee750c5aac01170a4be35: <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10-Isa.61.11">Isa 61:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13631" type="x-p"/> This is the joyful calling of the Servant of Jehovah to be the messenger of such promises of God to His people. <hi type="italic">“Joyfully I rejoice in Jehovah; my soul shall be joyful in my God, that He hath given me garments of salvation to put on, hath wrapped me in the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom who wears the turban like a priest, and as a bride who puts on her jewellery. For like the land which brings forth its sprouts, and as a garde which causes the things sown in it to sprout up; so the Lord Jehovah bringeth righteousness to sprouting, and renown before all nations.”</hi> The Targum precedes this last turn with “Thus saith Jerusalem.” But as <reference osisRef="Isa.61.4-Isa.61.9">Isa 61:4-9</reference> are a development of the glorious prospects, the realization of which has to be effected through the instrumentality of the person speaking in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3">Isa 61:1-3</reference> both in word and deed, the speaker here is certainly the same as there. Nor is it even the fact that he is here supposed to commence speaking again; but he is simply continuing his address by expressing at the close, as he did at the beginning, the relation in which he stands in his own person to the approaching elevation of His people. Exalted joy, which impels him to exult, is what he experiences in Jehovah his God (בּ denoting the ground and orbit of his experience): for the future, which so abounds in grace, and which he has to proclaim as a prophet and as the evangelist of Israel, and of which he has to lay the foundation as the mediator of Israel, and in which he is destined to participate as being himself an Israelite, consists entirely of salvation and righteousness; so that he, the bearer and messenger of the divine counsels of grace, appears to himself as one to whom Jehovah has given clothes of salvation to put on, and whom He has wrapped in the robe of righteousness. <hi type="italic">Tsedâqâh</hi> (righteousness), looked at from the evangelical side of the idea which it expresses, is here the parallel word to <hi type="italic">yeshū‛âh</hi> (salvation). The figurative representation of both by different articles of dress is similar to <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference> : <hi type="italic">yâ‛at</hi>, which only occurs here, is synonymous with <hi type="italic">‛âtâh</hi>, from which comes <hi type="italic">ma‛ăteh</hi>, a wrapper or cloak (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference>). He appears to himself, as he stands there hoping such things for his people, and preaching such things to his people, to resemble a bridegroom, who makes his turban in priestly style, i.e., who winds it round his head after the fashion of the priestly <hi type="italic">migbâ‛ōth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.9">Exo 29:9</reference>), which are called פּארים in <reference osisRef="Exod.39.28">Exo 39:28</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.18">Eze 44:18</reference>). Rashi and others think of the <hi type="italic">mitsnepheth</hi> of the high priest, which was of purple-blue; but יכהן does not imply anything beyond the <hi type="italic">migba‛âh</hi>, a tall mitra, which was formed by twisting a long linen band round the head so as to make it stand up in a point. כּהן is by no means equivalent to <hi type="italic">kōnēn</hi>, or <hi type="italic">hēkhı̄n</hi>, as Hitzig and Hahn suppose, since the verb <hi type="italic">kâhan</hi> = <hi type="italic">kūn</hi> only survives in <hi type="italic">kōhēn</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kı̄hēn</hi> is a denom., and signifies to act or play the priest; it is construed here with the accusative פּאר, which is either the accusative of more precise definition (“who play the priest in a turban;” A. ὡς νύμφιον ἱερατευόμενον στεφάνῳ), or what would answer better to the parallel member, “who makes the turban like a priest.” As often as he receives the word of promise into his heart and takes it into his mouth, it is to him like the turban of a bridegroom, or like the jewellery which a bride puts on (<hi type="italic">ta‛deh</hi>, <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, as in Hos 2:15). For the substance of the promise is nothing but salvation and renown, which Jehovah causes to sprout up before all nations, just as the earth causes its vegetation to sprout, or a garden its seed (כ as a preposition in both instances, <hi type="italic">instar</hi> followed by attributive clauses; see <reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">Isa 8:22</reference>). The word in the mouth of the servant of Jehovah is the seed, out of which great things are developed before all the world. The ground and soil (<hi type="italic">'erets</hi>) of this development is mankind; the enclosed garden therein (<hi type="italic">gannâh</hi>) is the church; and the great things themselves are <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>, as the true inward nature of His church, and <hi type="italic">tehillâh</hi> as its outward manifestation. The force which causes the seed to germinate is Jehovah; but the bearer of the seed is the servant of Jehovah, and the ground of his festive rejoicing is the fact that he is able to scatter the seed of so gracious and glorious a future.  <chapter eID="Isa.61"/> <div eID="gen13631" type="x-p"/>

                     </ns0:note> unto them that mourn in Zion <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Put by a <ns0:hi>Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tonymy</ns0:hi> for the Jews. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> among the Jews; and they for the Church of God, or, according to the Hebrew <ns0:hi>For</ns0:hi> Zion.</ns0:note>, to give unto them beauty for ashes <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>ashes</ns0:hi> under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand whatever is most proper for days of mourning, as Sackcloth sprinkled with Ashes, and these ashes which were sprinkled on their heads, mixing themselves with their tears, would render them of a woful Aspect, which was wont to be the habit of Mourners, as by <ns0:hi>Beauty</ns0:hi> whatever may be beautiful, or become times of rejoycing.</ns0:note>, the oyl of joy for mourning <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The sense is the same with the former, he calls it <ns0:hi>Oyl of joy</ns0:hi> in al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lusion to those anointings they were wont to use in times of joy, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 15. and also the same with what follows, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Gladness for heaviness, gladness brings forth Praise to God; and it is called a <ns0:hi>Gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment</ns0:hi> in allusion to their Festival Ornaments, for they had Garments appropriated to their conditions, some suitable to times of rejoy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cing, and some to times of mourning, or else an allusion to comely garments; and the <ns0:hi>spirit of heaviness,</ns0:hi> because heaviness doth op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />press, and debase the Spirits. It is all but an elegant description of the same thing by a three-fold Antithesis.</ns0:note>, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they might be called <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That is, that they may be so, as it is usually expressed. <ns0:hi>Ch</ns0:hi> 58. 12. & 60. 18. they shall be acknowledged so, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note> trees of righteousness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He ascribes Righteousness to Trees, understanding thereby Persons by a Metaphor, by which he means, that they shall be firm, solid, and well rooted, being by faith engraf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted into Christ, and bringing sorth fruit suitable to the Soil wherein they are planted, that had been as dry trees, see on <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 56. 3. <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Church, the Vineyard of God, and the hand by which they were planted, as in the next words.</ns0:note>, the planting of the LORD <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Planted by the holy Lord, who being himself holy, and righteous, would plant none but such, which notes also their soundness, and stability, an allusion to that passage in <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Song, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15. 17.</ns0:note>, that he might be glorified <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either in that glory which he should conser upon them, or that glory he may expect and receive from them, that so it may be evident whose handy work it was. See <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 60. 21.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And they shall <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 58. 12.</ns0:note> build the old wasts, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pair the wast cities, the desolations of many gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rations <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 58. 12. As it is applied to Gospel times, the meaning may be, that <ns0:hi>Gentilism,</ns0:hi> which was as a wilderness overgrown with Briars, and Thorns, shall be cultivated, and those Cities, and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vinces of the Gentiles, that lay as it were wast, void of all true Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligion, shall now by the Ministry of the Word, be edified in the true worship of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And strangers <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Viz. Gentiles,</ns0:hi> such as are not of the natural race of the Jews, but Gentile Converts. Or, such as shall have no more then an out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward profession, strangers to the true work of Grace.</ns0:note> shall stand <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Ready to be at thy service, a like expression, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 48. 13.</ns0:note> and feed your flocks <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Churches with the word of God.</ns0:note>, and the sons of the alien <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The same with <ns0:hi>strangers,</ns0:hi> or their suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessours.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> your plowmen, and your vine-dressers <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As the words describe the prosperous estate of the Jews, the meaning of them is, that they should be in such a flou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rishing and prosperous condition, that without their own labour, they should have all inferiour offices executed, either by slaves ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken in War, or by Persons hired for reward, which they should have Riches and Wealth enough to accomplish; But as they prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipally relate to the spiritual State of the Church, so probably by Strangers we may understand Converted Gentiles with their Suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessors meant by the <ns0:hi>Sons of Aliens,</ns0:hi> which should be ready to dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />charge all Offices for the advan<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>age of the Church feeding the Flocks, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Churches of Christ wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>h the Word of God, and should manage the whole work of God's Spiritual Husbandry there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in; see 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3. 6, 7, 8, 9. Or, by Strangers may be meant Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers of the Church onely by an outward Profession, even <ns0:hi>they</ns0:hi> shall be some way serviceable to her in ordinary and inferiour matters: <ns0:hi>The Earth shall help the Woman,</ns0:hi> Rev. 12. 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:623" />6 But ye shall be named the priests <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">For your part, <ns0:hi>ye</ns0:hi> emphatically shall be as Priests, Either, 1. For <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> as the Priests of old were plentifully provided for without their labour, so shall you by the labour of Strangers: Or, 2. For <ns0:hi>Countenance,</ns0:hi> you shall be every whereas greatly valued as the Priests were wont to be; you shall be esteemed as Princes; for so the word is often used, the word <ns0:hi>Priest</ns0:hi> being applied not onely to the Sacred Function, but to one that was of great note a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mong the People, and was supplied with all necessaries from others, without any labour of his own. Thus <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Sons were called <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Princes:</ns0:hi> Or rather, 3. For <ns0:hi>Priviledge,</ns0:hi> the whole body of them shall now be as peculiar, and as near to God as the Priests were formerly, and shall be a Royal Priesthood, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2. 9. This is most certainly true of all the faithful under the Gospel; hence they have also their Spiritual Sacrifices, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12. 1. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13. 15, 16. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2. 5.</ns0:note>

Rev. 1. 6. & 5. 10.</ns0:note> of the LORD: <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> shall call you the ministers of God: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 60. 6, 16.</ns0:note> ye shall eat <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">It relates to the Riches of the Gentiles, which did consist most in Flocks, and Herds: Or, what you eat shall be pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chased by the Riches of the Gentiles.</ns0:note> the riches of the Gentiles, and in their glory shall ye boast <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">You shall exalt your selves, or be renowned by others. The LXX render it, you shall be <ns0:hi>wonderful,</ns0:hi> or to <ns0:hi>admiration;</ns0:hi> or, grow high by the access of that glory, which they shall bring unto you, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Riches, Parts, Learn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, Chap.</ns0:hi> 60. 5, 11.</ns0:note> your selves.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. For your shame <ns0:hi>ye shall have</ns0:hi> double <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 40. 2.                         <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> of honour, that God will give them, the same thing with the former; or, in their Inheritance, which God shall restore to them; and that either, 1. For <ns0:hi>worth</ns0:hi> and value through God's blessing upon it: Or 2. For <ns0:hi>room</ns0:hi> and space, and that possibly by reason of the few that will return to inhabit there, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> onely a tenth part, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6. 13. Or, that which he shall give them out of their Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies Land.</ns0:note>: therefore <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>Because,</ns0:hi> being rendred as a reason of their rejoycing, because of the doubling of their portion, in which sense it is taken, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 14.</ns0:note> in their Land they shall possess the double: everlasting <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Of long continuance here, and everlasting hereafter; or, to be perpetually remembred on their Anniversary Festivals; though this had its accomplishment in their return from <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> yet was it most signally made good in that great change for the better, which they should find in the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel-state in the enlargement of Christ's Kingdom, and encrease of his People, with whom they should ever rejoyce together.</ns0:note> joy shall be unto them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 For I the LORD love judgment <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> They have suffered a great deal of hardship under their Enemies, and I will do them Right, for I love Justice in my self, and in them that practise it: Or, he gives a reason why he will recompense those Strangers that did<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> so freely minister to his People.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1. 13.</ns0:note> I hate robbery <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">All things gotten by injustice, though it be for Sacri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice: As God will not accept of that which cost nothing; so much less of that which is the Effect of Rapin, and Oppression; a foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation, whereon most of our Abbies and Monasteries were built, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to expiate some great Crimes. And thus by making God a <ns0:hi>Receiver,</ns0:hi> they did interpretatively make him a <ns0:hi>Confederate.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> for burnt-offerings, and I will <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>recom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pense.                         <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Though you have broken Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant with me, and I have seemed to forsake you in giving you up to Captivity, yet I will renew my ancient Covenant made with your Fathers, confirmed with the blood of Christ, and it shall be everlasting, never to be abrogated, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> it shall be continued in the Gentiles that shall come in your rooms, that for breach of Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nant were broken off.</ns0:note> with them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And their seed shall be among the Gentiles <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e. Eminently,</ns0:hi> a promise of the encrease of the Church; such shall be their prosperity, and multiplying, that they shall be known abroad by their great encrease; or else, the meaning is, the Church shall have a seed of the Gentiles, the borders of the Church shall be enlarged, whereas it hath been confined as it were to one corner of the world, now it shall remain in one Nation alone no more, but shall fill all the Nations of the Earth.</ns0:note>, and their off-spring among the People: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the seed which the LORD hath blessed <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">They shall be known to be the seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> partly by their holy conversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and partly by their exceeding blessings, it being the seed that the Lord had so often promised to bless: There shall be such visible Characters of God's love to them, & of God's grace in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 I will greatly rejoyce <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This by a Prosopopoeia is spoken in the Person of the Church, wherein she doth thankfully acknowledge God's kindness to her in the forementioned promises expressed here in the greatness of her affection with reference both to her present deliverance from <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon</ns0:hi> and to the happiness of her Gospel state.</ns0:note> in the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or because of the Lord, or of the goodness of the Lord towards me, an usual form of gratulation. 1. <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 1. and <ns0:hi>Hab.</ns0:hi> 3. 18. and <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1. 47. or thus, I will not rejoice so much in my deliverance, as in the Lord.</ns0:note>, my soul shall be joyful in my God <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This clause is to the same purpose, save only she varies the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Yea I do it with my whole Soul.</ns0:note>; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">With Salva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, as with a garment, so in the next with righteousness, as with a Robe, the meaning is the Salvation, that God will work for me, will render me as beautiful, and considerable, as they are, that are clothed with the richest garments, as Bridegrooms usually are, and Brides with their Jewels, or as venerable, as Kings in their Princely Robes, my Sac-cloath will now be turned into Robes or, I shall be compassed about with glory, as garments do compass the body.</ns0:note>, he hath cover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed me with the robe of righteousness <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Either with the fruits, and effects of his Love, and many Favours to the Church, in which sense <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> is taken, <ns0:hi>Psa.</ns0:hi> 112. 3, 4, 9. comp. with 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 9. and <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 51. 6, 8. she should see the <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> of God in fulfilling all these promises. Or that <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> of Christ imputed to us, which we are said to put on, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13. 14. or those graces imparted to us, and acted in an holy life.</ns0:note>, as a bride<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />groom <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>k<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth as a priest.</ns0:note> decketh <ns0:hi>himself</ns0:hi> with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth <ns0:hi>herself</ns0:hi> with her jewels.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 45. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">By this and the other Metaphor he shews not only the revi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of the blessings of the Church after they had been as it were dead in the winter of affliction, but the great plenty, and abundance of blessings that should break forth; that which had been as a wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness, shall be as a Paradise, pointing at the effects of his grace, and bounty.</ns0:note>: so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His great work of Salvation shall break out and appear.</ns0:note> and praise <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">As the natural product, and fruit of it, his own glory being the Principal end of making his Righteousness to appear and manifest its self.</ns0:note> to spring forth before all Nations <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">These things will not be done in a Corner, but will be eminently conspicuous in the sight of all the world, for which purpose those <ns0:hi>Hymns</ns0:hi> penned by the godly will ever be famous in the Churches of Christ to all ages, as of <ns0:hi>Moses, Hannah, Mary, Zechary, Simeon,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
